The South African pouched mouse Saccostomus campestris is a small, nocturnal rodent inhabiting savanna and scrubland regions of southern and eastern Africa, where it occupies a specialized ecological niche as a seed predator and opportunistic omnivore. Neonates are remarkably altricial at birth, with a wet weight of just 2.6 grams [Wwb = 2.6 grams], a value that underscores their underdeveloped state and complete dependence on maternal care during the first weeks of life. Under stable thermal conditions typical of laboratory rearing at a constant ambient temperature of 35.3 °C [T = 35.3 °C], females exhibit a gestation period lasting 21 days [tg = 21 days], which is relatively brief for a rodent of its adult body size and positions the species among the faster-reproducing members of the family Nesomyidae. This short intrauterine phase is energetically constrained by the mother's metabolic capacity and appears linked to the species' strategy of producing altricial, rapidly developing offspring. Following parturition, maternal investment continues intensively as the pups rely entirely on lactation for sustenance, a phase that culminates in nutritional independence at the time of weaning.

The weaning period represents a critical transition to nutritional independence for the altricial young of Saccostomus campestris. At an ambient temperature of 35.3 °C [T = 35.3 °C], the time since birth at weaning is 25 days (25 days since birth) [tx = 25 days since birth], though some field observations report a range of 20 to 25 days, suggesting minor variability depending on maternal condition and resource availability. By this age, the pups have achieved a wet weight of 12.5 grams [Wwx = 12.5 grams], representing a substantial increase from their neonatal mass but still far below adult dimensions. This phase of rapid somatic development relies heavily on the high energetic content of the mother's milk and is sensitive to environmental perturbations such as food scarcity, which can delay the weaning process. The relatively early acquisition of dietary independence allows females to produce multiple litters within a single breeding season, a key feature of this species' life history.

Sexual maturation in Saccostomus campestris proceeds at a moderate pace relative to other murid rodents of comparable size. Under controlled conditions maintained at 35.3 °C [T = 35.3 °C], the time since birth at puberty has been recorded at 45 days [tp = 45 days], after which individuals become reproductively viable. This relatively early onset of gonadal activity enables young born early in the breeding season to potentially contribute to reproduction within their first year of life, thereby increasing the population's intrinsic rate of increase. The attainment of reproductive maturity coincides with a period of continued somatic growth, as individuals have not yet reached their ultimate adult body mass at this stage. This decoupling of sexual and skeletal maturation is not uncommon among small mammals and likely reflects selective pressures for early reproduction in unpredictable environments.

The ultimate body mass attained by adult Saccostomus campestris shows considerable sexual dimorphism, with females typically reaching a larger size than males. Under optimum conditions in captivity, the ultimate wet weight recorded for this species is 61.3 grams [Wwi = 61.3 grams], although a secondary source reports a mean value of 47.4 grams [Wwi = 47.4 grams], suggesting population-level variation or differences in measurement protocols. This adult mass is modest among African murids and places the species in a small-bodied guild characterized by rapid life histories and high reproductive output. Basal metabolic rate measurements, obtained via open-flow respirometry at a standard ambient temperature of 35.3 °C [T = 35.3 °C] within the thermoneutral zone, yield a resting oxygen consumption of approximately 51.5 milliliters per hour [JOi = approximately 51.5 milliliters per hour]. This metabolic rate is consistent with allometric predictions for a mammal of this body size and supports a relatively high daily energy turnover that facilitates rapid growth and frequent reproduction.

Reproductive output in Saccostomus campestris is notably high for a rodent of its size, reflecting a strategy of iteroparity with multiple litters per year. Females typically produce litters containing 6.8 pups [N_R_i = litters containing 6.8 pups], and under favorable conditions at a constant temperature of 35.3 °C [T = 35.3 °C], they can achieve a maximum of approximately 3 litters each year [F_R_i = approximately 3 litters each year], amounting to a substantial annual fecundity. This high reproductive rate imposes significant energetic demands on lactating females, who must balance the costs of milk production with their own somatic maintenance. The maximum lifespan of Saccostomus campestris in captivity, recorded under standardized conditions at 35.3 °C [T = 35.3 °C], is approximately 4.5 years [am = approximately 4.5 years], which is relatively extended for such a small rodent and suggests a life-history strategy that, while heavily weighted toward early reproduction, still allows for multiple breeding seasons across a prolonged adult phase.
